The objective decides what the parameters `ps` and state `st` of a model look like, and
`setup(objective, rng, model, ...)` builds them accordingly. This page shows the four
objectives side by side on the theophylline data, together with the residual error models
that the likelihood-based ones need.

```{julia}
using DeepCompartmentModels
using DataFrames, CSV
using CairoMakie
using Random
using LinearAlgebra: diag

df = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "data", "theophylline.csv")))
population = Population([begin
    obs = g[.!ismissing.(g.DV), :]
    cb = generate_dosing_callback([0.0 g.AMT[1] * g.WEIGHT[1]])
    Individual(g.ID[1], [g.WEIGHT[1]], obs.TIME, obs.DV, cb)
end for g in groupby(df, :ID)])

ann = Lux.Chain(
    Normalize([100f0]), Lux.Dense(1, 8, tanh), Lux.Dense(8, 3, Lux.softplus),
    Lux.WrappedFunction(x -> x .* Float32[1, 3, 30]),
)
problem = ODEProblem(one_comp_abs!, zeros(Float32, 2), (-0.1f0, 1f0); dt = 0.01f0)
rng = Random.Xoshiro(1)
nothing # hide
```

## Fixed-effects objectives: SSE and MSE

`SSE()` and `MSE()` need no error model. The parameters contain only the network:

```{julia}
model = DCM(problem, ann; target = 2)
ps_sse, st_sse = setup(SSE(), rng, model)
keys(ps_sse), keys(st_sse)
```

Objectives are callables that return a scalar to minimise:

```{julia}
SSE()(model, population, ps_sse, st_sse), MSE()(model, population, ps_sse, st_sse)
```

`SSE` sums the squared residuals over all observations and `MSE` averages them per
individual first and then over the population. Both treat every observation as equally
informative, which is only appropriate if the noise is roughly constant.

## Residual error models

A likelihood needs an assumption about the noise. The error models describe the
standard deviation `σ` of an observation as a function of the prediction `ŷ`:

| model | variance | parameters |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `AdditiveError(σ)` | `σ²` | 1 |
| `ProportionalError(σ)` | `(σ ŷ)²` | 1 |
| `CombinedError([σ₁, σ₂])` | `σ₁² + (σ₂ ŷ)²` | 2 |
| `CombinedError([σ₁, σ₂]; dependent = true)` | `(σ₁ + σ₂ ŷ)²` | 2 |
| `CustomError` | your own `var` method | any |

The argument is the starting value. The parameters are stored on an unconstrained scale and
passed through a softplus, so they stay positive during optimisation. `make_dist` turns a
prediction into the distribution of the observations:

```{julia}
ŷ = Float32[0.5, 2, 8]
errors = [AdditiveError(0.5f0), ProportionalError(0.2f0), CombinedError(Float32[0.3, 0.1])]
ps_err = [setup(e, nothing) for e in errors]     # the initial parameters of each model

DataFrame(
    prediction = ŷ,
    additive = sqrt.(diag(var(errors[1], ŷ, ps_err[1], NamedTuple()))),
    proportional = sqrt.(diag(var(errors[2], ŷ, ps_err[2], NamedTuple()))),
    combined = sqrt.(diag(var(errors[3], ŷ, ps_err[3], NamedTuple()))),
)
```

```{julia}
make_dist(errors[2], ŷ, ps_err[2])
```

## Fixed effects with a likelihood

Give the model an error model and use `LogLikelihood()` to estimate the residual error
together with the network. The parameters gain an `error` entry:

```{julia}
model_ll = DCM(problem, ann, ProportionalError(0.2f0); target = 2)
ps_ll, st_ll = setup(LogLikelihood(), rng, model_ll)
keys(ps_ll), ps_ll.error
```

The objective is the negative log-likelihood. We first fit the network by least squares,
which gives a much better starting point than the random initialisation, and then
continue with the likelihood. The residual error `σ` is then free to adapt:

```{julia}
function train(objective, model, population, ps, st; epochs, lr)
    opt_state = Optimisers.setup(Optimisers.Adam(lr), ps)
    losses = Float32[]
    for _ in 1:epochs
        ∇ = gradient(objective, model, population, ps, st)
        opt_state, ps = Optimisers.update(opt_state, ps, ∇)
        push!(losses, objective(model, population, ps, st))
    end
    return ps, losses
end

ps_pre, _ = train(SSE(), DCM(problem, ann; target = 2), population, ps_sse, st_sse; epochs = 150, lr = 0.02f0)
ps_ll = merge(ps_ll, (theta = ps_pre.theta,))
ps_ll, losses = train(LogLikelihood(), model_ll, population, ps_ll, st_ll; epochs = 100, lr = 0.01f0)
(nll = losses[[1, end]], sigma = Lux.softplus.(ps_ll.error.σ))
```

The fitted `σ` is the estimated relative error of the proportional model. The negative
log-likelihood decreased while the network and `σ` were learned together.

## Random effects: the variational ELBO

`VariationalELBO(idxs)` adds random effects on the parameters listed in `idxs`, as shown
in the [mixed-effects tutorial](02-mixed-effects.md). It needs the population in `setup`,
because there is one variational posterior per individual:

```{julia}
objective = VariationalELBO([1, 2, 3])
ps_vi, st_vi = setup(objective, rng, model_ll, population)
(parameters = keys(ps_vi), state = keys(st_vi), posterior = keys(ps_vi.phi))
```

| entry | meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `ps.theta`, `st.theta` | the network weights and its state |
| `ps.error` | residual error parameters |
| `ps.omega` | covariance of the random effects |
| `ps.phi` | variational posterior per individual: means `μ` and Cholesky factors `L` |
| `st.phi` | `epsilon` (noise for sampling) and `mask`, which maps the random effects in `idxs` onto the ODE parameters |

The posterior and prior can be shaped with keyword arguments:

```{julia}
# a diagonal posterior per individual instead of a full covariance
ps_mf, _ = setup(VariationalELBO([1, 2, 3]; mean_field = true), rng, model_ll, population)
keys(ps_mf.phi), size(ps_mf.phi.σ[1])
```

```{julia}
# random effects on clearance and volume only, with a different starting variance
ps_cv, st_cv = setup(VariationalELBO([2, 3]), rng, model_ll, population; init_omega = [0.05, 0.2])
ps_cv.omega
```

`setup` also takes `params = MeanVar()` to store the posterior covariances directly instead
of as Cholesky factors (the default is `MeanSqrt()`), and `VariationalELBO` has options for the
path-derivative gradient estimator (`path_deriv`) and for natural-gradient training
(`natural`).

::: {.callout-note}
The element type of `ps` follows the `T` argument of `setup` (default `Float32`). Pass
`Float64` for double precision, but note that individuals and their dosing callbacks must
then be built with the same type.
:::

## Choosing an objective

| situation | objective |
|:--|:--|
| quick fit, constant noise, no uncertainty needed | `SSE()` or `MSE()` |
| noise depends on the concentration, or you need the residual error | `LogLikelihood()` with an error model |
| inter-individual variability, individual predictions | `VariationalELBO(idxs)` |
